children: Oil's roughly 40% surge since early August is quickly becoming an earnings risk for airlines and cruise operators, with crude futures challenging $110 per barrel and fuel-sensitive stocks already moving lower. The pressure is uneven: Carnival
look particularly exposed, while Royal Caribbean

For cruise operators, Carnival faces the clearest risk because it buys fuel largely at spot-market prices rather than relying on hedges. An industry study estimates that every 10% increase in fuel costs per metric ton can reduce Carnival's annual net income by as much as $140 million.

Royal Caribbean is better insulated. The company has hedged as much as 60% of its fuel needs at below-market prices, limiting the estimated annual net-income hit from a 10% fuel-price increase to roughly $50 million.
Viking carries even less exposure because of its smaller fleet and wealthier customer base, which gives it more flexibility to raise itinerary prices without materially hurting demand.

Delta owns an oil refinery in Pennsylvania, providing some protection from higher refining costs. American and United, however, no longer use fuel hedges, leaving both more directly exposed to price swings.
Bloomberg research estimates every one-cent increase in jet fuel prices adds roughly $46 million to American's annual operating expenses and about $40 million to United's.
Markets are already reflecting that concern. Since oil began surging in August, United shares have fallen about 18%, American 24%, and Delta 16%.
Fuel exposure is becoming one of the most important differentiators across travel stocks.
Investors should watch jet-fuel prices, hedging coverage, ticket and cruise pricing, and whether companies can pass higher costs onto customers without hurting demand.

Carnival, American and United face the most immediate margin pressure if oil stays near current levels. Royal Caribbean, Viking and Delta appear better protected, but sustained triple-digit oil would eventually test even stronger balance sheets and pricing power.

title: Airlines and Cruise Stocks Face New Oil Shock
